issues.issue: The execution date is left blank ("made as of June __, 2004"), so the date on which this Agreement took effect cannot be determined from its own words. A court would have to construe when, or whether, the instrument became operative as between LSB and DMSA.

"Control" is defined only as the "power to direct or cause the direction of the management and policies of a Person," with no ownership threshold or other boundary. Whether a given DMSA entity is an "Affiliate" for purposes of Section 12.7's outside-business licence therefore has no determinate answer.

Capital Contribution is measured by "the fair market value of any property (other than money) contributed," but neither this definition nor Schedule A states who values non-cash contributions or when. DMSA's initial capital under the Venture Agreement was to include travel, legal fees and staff labor, so the valuation gap has real work to do.

"Covered Person" sweeps in every Affiliate, officer, employee, representative or agent of a Member, which makes the indemnity in Section 12.4 run to persons who are strangers to the Agreement. Its outer boundary ("representatives") is undefined.

Clause (iii) refers to "the period described in Clause (ii) of this sentence," but the clauses are mis-numbered in the text ((i), (11), (iii)), so which period is cross-referenced is uncertain. The mechanical numbering error changes what a partial Fiscal Year is.

The definition of "Interest" is internally garbled — "such Member's interest of the profits and losses" — and bundles voting, profit and distribution rights without saying whether a transfer of one carries the others. Article XVI's transfer machinery turns on exactly that.

The enumeration of "Laws" ends with the open-ended category "all policies, practices and guidelines of any governmental body," which is far broader than the binding instruments listed before it. Whether non-binding agency guidance counts as "Law" for provisions such as Section 9.3 is left unresolved.

"Majority" is defined as a quantity of Member Votes, yet Section 5.5(vii) speaks of "A Majority present in person or by proxy" as if it were a person. The definition cannot be substituted into the operative text without incoherence.

"Members" is defined as "two (2) or more of such Persons," so provisions conditioned on action by "the Members" (e.g. Sections 2.4 and 8.2(i)) arguably require both LSB and DMSA acting together rather than a Majority Vote. With only two members the plural definition and the voting provisions pull apart.

Member Votes are whatever Schedule A "as may be amended" says, but this definition names no procedure or consent requirement for amending Schedule A, while Section 17.10 requires unanimity for amendments and Section 2.1(iii) lets the Secretary update Schedule A unilaterally. How voting power can lawfully be changed is therefore in doubt.

Net Cash Flow is reduced by "any amounts determined by the Members to be necessary to provide a reasonable reserve," yet Section 9.2 commits the timing and amount of all distributions to the Board. Whether Members or the Board set reserves cannot be squared from the two provisions.

Percentage Interest is fixed "as shown on Schedule A" but simultaneously "as determined by the unanimous written consent of the Members as adjusted from time to time," which does not square with Section 2.1(iii) authorising the Secretary to update Schedule A without member consent. Which mechanism governs an adjustment of ownership is unresolved.

The list of entities in "Person" uses the defined term "Company," which Article I fixes as Dialogo, LLC itself, evidently in place of "corporation." Read literally, the definition of Person excludes corporations generally.

Profits and Losses are defined purely as taxable income or loss under § 703(a), with none of the book adjustments that Section 4.4(ii) and Section 8.2(iv) presuppose by requiring Capital Accounts and allocations to comply with Treasury Regulation § 1.704-1(b) and Code § 704(b). The tax definition and the 704(b) capital-account regime cannot both be applied as written.

Membership is made to turn on "execution of this Agreement or a counterpart," but the instrument as filed bears a blank date and no executed signature page. Whether LSB and DMSA ever became Members under this provision is a live question.

This provision says a revision to Schedule A "shall not be deemed an amendment to this Agreement," while Schedule A fixes Percentage Interests, Member Votes and Capital Contributions that Section 17.10 makes amendable only by unanimous written vote of all Members. The two provisions cannot both be given effect if the Secretary revises Schedule A alone.

The provision obliges "Gerry Pike," a person who is not a party to the Agreement and holds no office defined in it, to execute and file the Articles. Whose obligation this is if Pike does not act is unstated.

The power to designate a new registered agent or office is given to "the Members," whereas Section 2.6 gives the Board the corresponding qualification and filing functions and Section 5.1 leaves the Members no power to bind the Company individually. Who may change the agent, and by what vote, is not squared.

The Secretary is directed to file qualification certificates for any jurisdiction "in which the Company may wish to conduct business," while the preceding sentence ties the duty to jurisdictions where it "transacts business." The two standards fix different triggers within the same section.

The stated object — "developing Spanish language newspaper(s) and media" — is immediately swallowed by the general "any lawful act or activity for which limited liability companies may be formed," so the specific purpose sets no boundary on the Company's field. That boundary matters because Section 12.7 makes LSB's exclusivity run to "the business" and DMSA free to compete outside it.

Merger requires "approval of all of the Members," but Section 6.8 vests decisions on dispositions of assets and equity issuances in a unanimous Board and Section 6.1 gives the Board management of the business generally. Whether a merger also needs Board action is left open.

The recitation that each Member "has contributed or is deemed to have contributed" the Schedule A amount cannot be squared with Schedule A itself, which lists LSB at the garbled figure "$00,001.00," and with the Venture Agreement's acknowledgement that LSB would contribute no cash. What LSB in fact contributed for her 49% is unresolved.

No Member may be required to make additional capital contributions, which does not square with the Venture Agreement's provision that DMSA "shall contribute the initial capital to launch the LLC" in an amount DMSA deems appropriate. Whether DMSA's funding commitment survives this Agreement is a question of which instrument governs.

Returns of Capital Contributions must be made "to all Members in proportion to their Percentage Interests," which cannot be squared with Section 6.8(iii) permitting distributions only "to reimburse DMSA for initial capital contributions." A repayment of DMSA's launch capital is either a pro-rata return or a DMSA-only reimbursement, not both.

Exception (a) — "the respective invoices of each of DMSA" — is grammatically incomplete, so it cannot be told whether the payment right belongs to DMSA alone or to each of DMSA and LSB. Exception (b) then pays profits per "Membership Interests," a term the Agreement never defines.

The bar on any Member receiving salary or compensation for services conflicts with Section 12.7's requirement that LSB "employ its diligent efforts for the Company" exclusively, and with the Venture Agreement's designation of LSB as Publisher running day-to-day operations. Whether LSB could be paid for full-time service is exactly what these provisions leave unsettled.

The phrase "the Members shall be able only to make their capital contributions pursuant to Section 4.1" is garbled — "be able only" reads as a prohibition where an obligation limit was intended. Whether it forbids further contributions that Section 4.1(ii) expressly permits by unanimous consent is the resulting question.
